Introduction Mucopolysaccharidosis type I H (MPS IH; Hurler syndrome) is a rare autosomal recessive disease that causes deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase – an enzyme responsible for catabolizing glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). While historically considered a pediatric disease with an overall median life expectancy of 8.7 years, advances in MPS IH treatment options have extended patient lifespans into adulthood; however, long-term progression of MPS IH currently remains minimally described. This study aims to provide a comprehensive literature review about the adult disease burden of MPS IH as validated by a medical records analysis of an adult patient with MPS IH. Methods A comprehensive literature review was conducted to establish foundational information about the mechanism of action, clinical presentation, diagnostic complexity, treatment, and knowledge gaps of MPS IH. Medical records of a 32-year-old patient with MPS IH were analyzed, and a chronology of major clinical events was constructed to demonstrate the multi-system disease burden of MPS IH in pediatric, adolescent, and adult survivorship timelines. Results Lysosomal GAG accumulation causes onset of musculoskeletal deformities, facial and dental variations, cardiopulmonary complications, neurocognitive manifestations, and other systematic developments in MPS IH patients – all of which progress in severity over time. The patient case analysis highlights these sequelae in addition to development of dural meningiomas, thought to have resulted from childhood total body irradiation performed before hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, that required multiple craniotomy resections and gamma knife radiosurgeries and triggered seizure activity. Conclusion This study provides a comprehensive, literature-based, clinical narrative about the adult disease burden of MPS IH as validated by a unique patient case analysis. While childhood treatments may extend MPS IH patient life expectancy, they may not prevent progressive development of common sequelae or adult-stage neuro-oncologic developments. This study may enhance physician awareness about the multi-system adult disease burden of MPS IH, improve treatment and long-term surveillance strategies for MPS IH survivors, and support clinical counseling for families affected by MPS IH. Highlights • A comprehensive literature-based review about MPS IH and its clinical implications. • Impacts of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation as childhood treatment for MPS IH. • Chronology of major clinical events from analysis of MPS IH patient medical records. • Neuro-oncologic disease progression as key finding in adult MPS IH disease burden. • Pre- and post- operational MRI of a meningioma in an adult patient with MPS IH. This triggers a cascade of pathogenic effects for cells that synthesize or ingest them, including defects in cellular transport and degradation, oxidative stress, and auto-inflammatory responses across multiple systems, each resulting in irreversible cell damage. Severe manifestations can include organ failure, cognitive impairments, and shortened lifespan [1] , [2] . There are nine MPS disorders numbered according to their approximate chronological identification: MPS I (with Hurler syndrome, Hurler-Scheie syndrome, and Scheie syndrome subtypes) [3] , MPS II (Hunter syndrome) [4] , MPS III (Sanfilippo syndrome with three subtypes) [5] , MPS IV (Morquio syndrome with two subtypes) [6] , MPS VI (Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome) [7] , MPS VII (Sly syndrome), MPS IX (hyaluronidase deficiency) [8] , MPSPS (mucopolysaccharidosis-plus syndrome) [9] , and MPS X (arylsulfatase K deficiency) [10] . While each MPS disorder is caused by specific enzymatic deficiency leading to a buildup of GAGs, their clinical presentations vary widely. 1.2 MPS type I disorders MPS type I is characterized by a clinically significant deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase (α-L-iduronidase), an IDUA hydrolase enzyme that breaks down dermatan sulphate and heparan sulphate in the lysosomal storage pathway [11] . The incidence of MPS I is approximately 1 in 100,000 births [12] , [13] . Though no difference in prevalence is indicated between males and females, MPS I incidence differs between populations due to its heritability. For example, Puckett et al. [14] calculated an incidence ranging from 0.11 per 100,000 live births in Taiwan, 0.26 per 100,000 in the United States, and 1.85 per 100,000 in Norway. MPS type I presents as a spectrum disorder, differentiated by symptom severity. The severe phenotype is known as Hurler syndrome (MPS IH; OMIM 607014 ), and other forms are classified as attenuated MPS I (Hurler-Scheie syndrome, MPS IH-S, OMIM 607015 ; Scheie syndrome, MPS IS, OMIM 607016 ). The prevalence distribution among these MPS I phenotypes is 60.9% MPS IH, 35.9% attenuated MPS I (MPS IA) subtypes, and 3.2% undetermined [12] . Notably, the severe phenotype, MPS IH, accounts for the majority of MPS I diagnoses [13] . In a study about MPS prevalence and survival in a United Kingdom population, the MPS IH subtype appeared over two times more frequently than the attenuated subtypes [15] . Genetically, MPS I results from biallelic pathogenic variants of the IDUA gene. All subtypes share this genetic basis, though the specific mutations and resulting enzymatic activity differ. A phenotypic continuum exists in which homozygosity or compound heterozygosity for pathogenic variants results in the severe MPS IH phenotype, and the presence of at least one missense variant results in attenuated MPS IA. While nomenclature has historically divided MPS IA into two subtypes (Hurler-Scheie and Scheie syndromes), no biochemical differences are present between these subtypes; the differentiation exists only as a historical delineation of the variable phenotypic presentations of MPS I [16] . While IDUA gene variations result in altered enzymatic activity, clinically benign variants may not reduce α-L-iduronidase activity within pathological margins [17] . Particularly, the presence of in cis variants has been tied to benign presentations, known as pseudodeficiency variants, that significantly alter enzymatic activity but do not result in MPS I disorders [18] . Therefore, genetic testing alone is not conclusive for MPS I diagnosis and must be paired with a clinically significant elevation of GAGs. 1.3 History of MPS I MPS II was the first MPS identified by Charles Hunter in 1917, who described two brothers with atypical musculoskeletal characteristics [4] , [19] . In 1920, Dr. Gertrud Hurler described two other cases with a clinical presentation similar to that described by Hunter [20] . In these cases, the patients presented with short stature, severe kyphosis, skeletal deformities (including a macrocephalic skull with extra bones), and corneal clouding. At the time, the four cases were considered as one disease since their presentations overlapped, though Hurler's cases were distinguishable by the severe kyphosis (gibbus) and corneal clouding which were later recognized as features specific to MPS I. In the following years, MPS I was described under a variety of terms. In 1936, Ellis et al. [21] coined the term Gargoylism to describe the condition; however, due to its negative connotations, the term was deprecated in the 1950s and 1960s in favor of Hurler's disease [22] . As the clinical picture of Hurler's disease stabilized, Brante [23] proposed a biochemical cause of the disease in 1952, noting the build-up of material deposits within various cells. In 1962, ophthalmologist Harold Scheie noted a new forme fruste , or attenuated form, of Hurler's disease, first classified as MPS V [24] . In 1968, a Hurler's disease corrective factor was identified in co-cultures of Hurler and Hunter disease cells that could break down the accumulated material deposits [25] . This experiment demonstrated that cells could secrete the missing lysosomal enzyme for uptake by neighboring cells, establishing the principle of cross-correction, which later became foundational to contemporary treatments. In 1972, Bach et al. [26] , [27] identified this corrective factor as α-L-iduronidase, a deficiency of which is common in both Hurler and Scheie syndromes. At the time, the distinction between the phenotypic variants was thought to arise from mutations in different genes, and the intermediate Hurler-Scheie form represented heterozygosity at each gene. This model was later disproved once the IDUA gene was cloned, confirming that the MPS I subtypes represent a clinical continuum caused by more than 100 pathogenic alleles of the same gene. Following this discovery, MPS I has been recharacterized as a spectrum disorder with severe (MPS IH) and attenuated (MPS IA) forms [1] , [28] . 1.4 Clinical presentation of MPS I Although MPS IH represents the most severe MPS I type, children born with MPS IH may initially be asymptomatic as the disease develops progressively during infancy and childhood [13] . Symptoms typically present within 6 months, with diagnosis occurring 6 months after symptom onset and treatment beginning shortly thereafter [29] . MPS IA progresses more slowly, with a median age at MPS I diagnosis ranging from 5 to 10 years. Despite earlier diagnosis from earlier indications of disease onset, the median lifespan for untreated MPS IH patients is under 10 years [15] , whereas the median lifespan for untreated MPS IA patients is longer, with the majority of patients living into adulthood [15] , [30] . Progressive onset of signs and symptoms of MPS IH includes a spectrum of musculoskeletal deformities, facial and dental variations, cardiopulmonary complications, neurocognitive manifestations, and other systematic developments. 1.4.1 Musculoskeletal variations Numerous musculoskeletal manifestations characterize MPS IH. Collectively, they are referred to as dysostosis multiplex [31] and result from dysfunctional primary ossification, bone remodeling, ligaments, and joint capsules. Observed presentations include short stature, coarse facial features, kyphosis, hip dysplasia, claw hand, genu valgum, dental irregularities, and carpal tunnel syndrome [32] . Craniovertebral joint variations may be present, including odontoid hypoplasia which can lead to life-threatening spinal cord compression [33] . Additionally, MPS IH causes impaired growth due to GAG deposits in the epiphyseal plates, macrocephaly from calvarial thickening, enlarged cerebral structures, and accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid [34] . The skeletal disease burden of MPS IH is particularly severe. GAG accumulation in cartilage and bone disrupts chondrocyte maturation, growth plate formation, and endochondral ossification, leading to progressive deformities of dysostosis multiplex [34] . In the first 6 months after birth, limited skeletal abnormalities may be present, including thoracolumbar kyphosis and scoliosis, as well as subtle facial coarsening. After 6 months, specific symptoms develop, increasing disease morbidity [35] , [36] . Although MPS I treatment options are available, they offer limited effectiveness in decreasing the burden of skeletal manifestations. Due to their low permeability and lack of chondrocyte vasculature, bone and cartilage receive insufficient enzymes utilized in therapies. Additionally, permanent tissue damage may occur early in life, before treatment, and cannot be reversed with current treatment options. While treatments cannot correct preexisting damage, early intervention with combined hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) has been shown to limit the progression of skeletal disease and improve bone growth [34] , [37] . 1.4.2 Facial and dental variations Facial variations associated with MPS IH result from a combination of skeletal dysplasia and soft-tissue GAG deposition, leading to characteristic craniofacial and dental alterations. Coarsening facial features is often observable at birth and progresses through development. Other deviations include macrocephaly and nasal variations such as depressed nasal bridge, broad nasal tip, anteverted nostrils, and narrowed nasal passages [38] . Such features are commonly associated with genetic defects and many other lysosomal storage diseases [39] . Additionally, changes in palatal anatomy result in delayed dental growth, improper spacing, misshapen teeth, and gingival hyperplasia, which together with nasal variations predispose patients to further complications. Other oral variations include decreased motion at the temporomandibular joint and reduced growth of the maxillary width, mandibular height, and mandibular length [40] . 1.4.3 Cardiopulmonary complications Life-threatening comorbidities of MPS IH include upper and lower airway obstructions caused by GAG deposition leading to macroglossia, adenotonsillar hypertrophy, and tracheobronchial narrowing. Variations in the upper airway present increased risk for airway obstruction, upper and lower respiratory tract infections, pulmonary hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea syndrome, cor pulmonale, and complications during anesthesia [13] , [41] , [42] , [43] , [44] . As it exists in about 75% of patients with MPS I, obstructive sleep apnea caused by adenoid hyperplasia presents a serious respiratory problem early in life, and craniofacial features such as maxillary constriction, macroglossia, and midface hypoplasia further contribute to airway compromise [45] . However, HSCT therapy has been shown to minimize the risk by ameliorating adenoid hyperplasia and maxillary constriction [41] . Despite improvements, residual lung disease remains a prominent issue for MPS IH patients. Even with treatment, decreased pulmonary capacity can be further exacerbated by diaphragmatic restriction secondary to hepatosplenomegaly, contributing to progressive loss of pulmonary function. Cardiovascular disease adds additional strain to the already compromised cardiopulmonary system, contributing significantly to morbidity and mortality, with cardiac involvement estimated to play a role in up to 50% of deaths in untreated MPS IH [46] . MPS-related vasculopathy is characterized by GAG deposition within arterial walls, leading to coronary narrowing. Imaging studies have demonstrated increased carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) contributing to increased arterial stiffness and decreased elasticity [47] . Valvular heart disease is highly prevalent, especially of the mitral valve, where GAG accumulation leads to nodular thickening of valve leaflets, chordae tendineae shortening, valvular insufficiency, and endocardial fibroelastosis, collectively impairing cardiac blood flow [13] , [48] . Furthermore, recent studies suggest that treatments are not completely effective in halting vasculopathy, contributing to the substantial cardiovascular morbidity in these patients [47] . The combination of progressive airway disease, restrictive lung impairment, and escalating cardiac dysfunction establishes cardiopulmonary failure as the leading cause of mortality in the first decade of life in patients with MPS IH [49] . 1.4.4 Neurocognitive manifestations Neuroanatomy and neurocognitive development are significantly impaired by GAG accumulation in MPS IH. White and gray matter changes, ventriculomegaly, hydrocephalus, cortical atrophy, and enlargement of the perivascular spaces have all been commonly identified in MPS disorders [50] . In severe cases of MPS IH, such effects have been associated with chronic progression of intellectual disability in patients, regardless of treatment [51] . Patients typically experience normal neurological development during the first few months of life followed by a slowing by 12 months and reaching a plateau in cognitive development by 2 to 4 years [52] . A subsequent rapid decline in cognitive development is concurrent with a lifelong below-average IQ [42] . While early implementation of HSCT treatment can limit this progression, patients still present with lower-than-average IQ, and therapy cannot currently reverse any decline that has already occurred [52] . 1.4.5 Other systemic manifestations Prominent systemic manifestations of MPS IH reflect widespread GAG accumulation throughout the body. GAG build-up within the vascular endothelium, reticuloendothelial cells, and leukocytes contributes to the high prevalence of hepatosplenomegaly, leading to abdominal distention and diaphragmatic restriction. Additionally, recurrent umbilical and inguinal hernias are among the earliest signs of MPS IH due to connective tissue weakness and often require surgical repair [16] . Auditory involvement, characterized by conductive hearing loss and eustachian tube dysfunction, represents a common cause of hearing loss in MPS IH [53] . A prominent ocular complication of MPS IH is corneal clouding which is attributed to the accumulation of GAGs that alter corneal collagen formation; however, serological treatments remain ineffective due to the avascularity of the cornea [54] . Glaucoma, optic neuropathy, and retinopathy represent additional ocular sequelae [55] , [56] . These systemic findings underscore the multi-system disease burden of MPS IH and reinforce the need for chronic, longitudinal, and multispecialty monitoring. 1.5 Diagnosis Due to the progressive nature of MPS I, early diagnosis is critical in providing favorable patient outcomes. Several techniques are utilized, and the specificity of diagnosis is improving. However, while a 2020 review found that the interval between diagnosis and treatment has improved since 2003, the median age at diagnosis has remained essentially unchanged [57] . This presents an emphasis for future research on how to provide earlier diagnoses. From the early to mid-1900s, clinical observation of symptoms was the primary method of diagnosis for MPS I. Prevalent symptoms that begin to present after 6 months of age include rhinitis, recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, hepatosplenomegaly, recurrent hernias, and mild thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis. However, MPS IH presentation is like other MPS I disorders where, as diagnosis is delayed and more specific symptoms develop, the disease burden increases and patient outcomes suffer [29] , [30] . As understanding of MPS I improved, quantification of urinary GAGs emerged for screening MPS disorders [58] and direct enzyme activity was analyzed in fibroblasts and peripheral leukocytes [16] , [42] . While these dye assays were available for accurate screening and early diagnosis, they were slow and required fresh cell handling for analysis. Methods with higher accuracy such as dried blood spot enzyme assays for measuring α-L-iduronidase activity were developed in the early 2000s [59] . This method enabled specific measurement of IDUA enzyme activity, making newborn screening possible; however, it suffers from high false-positive rates and requires secondary confirmation by urinalysis and internal disaccharide liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry for GAGs or IDUA gene sequencing. IDUA gene sequencing, while confirmatory, cannot reliably predict phenotype severity, as many pseudodeficiencies are non-pathogenic [16] . Therefore, dried blood spot analysis remains the primary diagnostic method for obtaining accurate results. In recent years, a new second-tier GAG biomarker test has been developed that examines disease-specific endogenous non-reducing ends that accumulate due to IDUA deficiency. Although not yet available globally, it reduces the false-positive rate of dried blood spot analysis, offering a more reliable distinction between true IDUA deficiency and pseudodeficiency. Expanded adoption of this method may help decrease the persistent delay between disease onset and diagnosis, particularly in attenuated cases where early symptoms are subtle [60] . 1.6 Treatment Treatment and management of MPS IH is challenging due to the systemic and progressive nature of the disease. Combination therapy of HSCT and ERT forms the foundation of current disease-modifying treatments. Emerging gene therapy techniques aim to provide more sustained enzyme delivery while surgical and supportive interventions remain significant in addressing the range of clinical manifestations. Nevertheless, even with early and appropriate treatment, patients with MPS IH continue to face a substantial disease burden and require ongoing efforts to manage the syndrome's effects [35] . 1.6.1 Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation Allogeneic HSCT serves as the current standard of care for children diagnosed with MPS IH. When performed in the first 2.5 years of life, HSCT treatment is most effective and can reduce the disease's burden and progression, though it does not reverse damage [34] . In 1980, the first documented HSCT procedure for MPS IH was performed on a one-year-old who received a bone marrow graft from their father and mother [61] . Since then, HSCT has become the standard for effective treatment of MPS IH. Moore et al. [15] report the impacts of HSCT in MPS IH patients, indicating significantly extended lifespan for patients who received a bone marrow transplant (mean 15.6 years) compared to those who did not (mean 7.9 years). In 2004, the first unrelated donor umbilical cord blood transplantation was performed as an alternative to bone marrow for HSCT [62] . Unrelated umbilical cord blood transplantation offers faster availability, reduced donor risk, greater enzyme delivery, more tolerant matching, and a lower risk of graft rejection, making it a more effective and accessible HSCT option [63] . It also reduces secondary risks of bone disease although it may not be available for all patients [64] , [65] . A few mechanisms contribute to the effectiveness of HSCT. Progressive clinical improvement as donor-derived cells develop provides initial benefit to patients as the new functional cell population expands. Moreover, α-L-iduronidase is secreted from transplanted cells into the extracellular space for uptake by nearby cells, in a process known as cross-correction, thereby significantly contributing to GAG storage clearance [42] . Although significant long-term improvements are noted after HSCT treatment, notably including survival into the third decade of life and improved cognitive and growth impacts, there are still many limitations. Since HSCT therapy cannot reverse established damage, early intervention is critical. Despite its benefits, the procedure carries a substantial acute risk, and engraftment can be slow or incomplete due to donor chimerism. Cellular delivery to the central nervous system is inefficient, and donor cells take a long time to reach the brain. Skeletal manifestations often persist due to limited bone penetrance and require long-term monitoring for secondary risk factors. While HSCT carries significant acute risks, its durable systemic effects justify its use in treating MPS IH [29] , [34] , [42] , [66] , [67] , [68] , [69] . 1.6.2 Enzyme replacement therapy ERT provides temporary enzyme supplementation rather than a long-term cellular source and requires repeated infusions that result in a time-limited therapeutic impact. In ERT, intravenous delivery of Laronidase (human recombinant α-L-iduronidase) presents the enzyme into the blood for cross-correction in deficient cells. Although it is quickly depleted and requires weekly therapy, it offers several benefits over HSCT [30] . ERT has been shown to provide the greatest benefits in highly vascularized organs, reversing hepatosplenomegaly and improving cardiopulmonary manifestations [70] . Additionally, ERT is more accessible in regions without HSCT capabilities. It can be used during the peri-transplant period to strengthen HSCT eligibility and reduce graft-versus-host disease, and unlike HSCT, ERT can be used later in life to ease disease progression and symptoms [30] . Although ERT is an effective, safe, and accessible acute therapy, its limited ability to treat severe complications, especially those associated with MPS IH, may limit its use as a standalone treatment [70] , [71] . The enzyme provided in ERT does not cross the blood-brain barrier sufficiently to impact the central nervous system biomarkers; therefore, in cases of attenuated MPS I, this limitation is less impactful [36] . However, in MPS IH cases, ERT groups have shown substantially greater incidence of adverse central nervous system outcomes, including cervical spinal cord compression and hydrocephalus, when compared to groups treated with HSCT [72] . ERT is also less efficient than HSCT at improving joint range-of-motion, dysostosis multiplex, cardiac vulvopathology, and corneal clouding [70] . Although safe, the chronic use of intravenous therapy becomes expensive as it is not curative, and patients may still require additional interventions [73] . 1.6.3 Surgical interventions and multidisciplinary care Surgical interventions and multidisciplinary care are essential components of supportive management for patients with MPS IH. Surgical interventions are used to correct disease manifestations and reduce secondary complications, including orthopedic, corneal, cardiac, airway, and cancer management [34] . Furthermore, even after HSCT treatment, many musculoskeletal manifestations continue to persist and develop especially considering the development of children with the disease [32] . Spinal irregularities relating to severe kyphosis and atlantoaxial instability carry high risks in life-threatening spinal cord compression and require procedures such as the growing rod technique for correction [74] . While surgical procedures inherently carry risk of complication, multidisciplinary management of symptoms may also be utilized. For example, physical therapy offers a non-surgical treatment option to maintain or improve motor abilities [75] . 1.6.4 Experimental therapies Many experimental therapies are being studied for their potential to treat MPS IH beyond conventional methods of ERT and HSCT [35] , [76] . Anti-inflammatory drugs such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) inhibitors and other immunomodulators are being tested for their ability to reduce inflammatory markers that contribute to joint pathology and pain [77] , [78] , [79] . Alternative routes for enzyme delivery, including intrathecal and intracerebroventricular administration, may provide greater neurological outcomes by bypassing the blood-brain barrier [80] . Additionally, new targeted drug delivery systems have higher specificity and improved localization utilizing monoclonal antibody-conjugated fusion proteins or nano-targeted therapies such as nanoparticles, nano-emulsions, liposomes, or micelles [81] , [82] . Fusing α-L-iduronidase to transporters to cross the blood-brain barrier could prove effective [83] , and due to their small size (less than 50 kilodaltons), pharmaceutical chaperones could also improve outcomes across the blood-brain and blood-retinal barriers in certain mutations [76] . Gene-editing-based treatments are also in clinical trials to improve perfusion in poorly accessible regions. These treatments generally include the introduction of viral gene therapies, using retroviruses, lentiviruses, and adeno-associated viruses, or nonviral strategies to edit hematopoietic stem cell lines [76] . Among these treatments, ex vivo lentivirus and in vivo adeno-associated virus therapies have shown the greatest improvement, especially when combined with autologous stem cell therapy (NIH Clinical Trials NCT03488394 and NCT03580083 ). Trials have shown greater improvements in cognitive, ocular, auditory, and skeletal impairments than typically observed with current standard therapies [84] , [85] . Substrate reduction therapies also hold promise for reducing GAG synthesis, thereby restoring the natural balance between GAG synthesis and degradation in MPS cells [86] . 1.7 Study motivation and objective Given the rarity, clinical severity, and diagnostic complexity of MPS IH cases, there is still critical information that has yet to be discovered about the unique disease. While the untreated median life expectancy of patients with MPS IH is under 10 years, modern advances in MPS IH treatment options have been shown to extend patient lifespans into the third decade of life (adulthood); however, MPS IH survivorship and long-term MPS IH progression consequently remain minimally described especially in regard to new sequelae developed by adult MPS IH patients. Based on the literature-based introduction to MPS I disorders, the aim of this study is to provide a comprehensive clinical narrative about the adult disease burden of MPS IH as validated and contextualized by a records analysis of a 32-year-old patient with MPS IH. The medical record review and chronological mapping of comorbidities are projected to highlight persistent knowledge gaps about MPS IH survivors. While this case does not represent the oldest case of MPS I survivorship, its analysis and associated discussion are intended to provide important perspectives on the extended disease trajectory for a condition historically considered as only pediatric. By synthesizing multi-system complications across 32 years of survival, this article may enhance awareness of adult MPS IH presentations and expand educational understanding of long-term disease manifestation. Results from this study may advance physician knowledge, inform treatment plans for patients with MPS IH, and support clinical counseling for families affected by MPS IH. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Literature review A targeted but comprehensive online review of clinical literature regarding MPS I disorders was conducted to establish foundational knowledge about MPS IH disease progression (clinical presentation, diagnosis, treatment, etc.) and identify any documented outcomes from reports of existing adult MPS IH survivors. The literature review provided an informed basis for interpreting the MPS IH case records and conveying its subsequent clinical discussion. Accessible articles describing directly or translationally relevant information about MPS I were included. Articles for which the authors were unable to obtain the full text and articles not written in the English language were excluded. 2.2 Patient consent, ethical approval, and compliance An adult MPS IH patient and his legal guardians provided personal, conscious and cognizant, written informed consent for the patient's medical records to be analyzed and disseminated as part of this study. The authors completed training to handle the information in this study in a safe, secure, and respectful manner. The protocol for this study was reviewed by the Institutional Review Board at the affiliated institution and approved under 45 CFR 46.104 (IRB-2024-186). All procedures were performed in compliance with relevant laws and institutional guidelines. 2.3 Case analysis The adult MPS IH patient was identified through a pre-established network. Relevant medical records were provided by the patient's legal guardians, from which a longitudinal chronology of major clinical events was constructed to demonstrate the multi-system disease burden of MPS IH in pediatric, adolescent, and adult survivorship timelines ( Fig. 1 ). All records were anonymized of personally identifiable information immediately upon receipt. Multiple magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) files were reviewed and composited to visually demonstrate the adult onset of meningiomas associated with MPS IH treatment and survivorship ( Fig. 2 ) and anatomical morphology associated with MPS IH development ( Fig. 3 ). All MRI sequence parameters were reported in their respective figure images. 3 Case description 3.1 Chronology of pediatric and adolescent clinical events The present case involves a 32-year-old male patient with MPS IH. The patient was diagnosed with MPS IH in infancy and underwent a blood transfusion in the same year ( Fig. 1 A). At 15 months old, the patient underwent single-fraction total body irradiation prior to conditioning for bone marrow-derived HSCT. After graft rejection, the patient successfully underwent a second HSCT eight months later. The patient did not receive ERT at any point during treatment. At 5 years old, the patient underwent cataract surgery to treat lens impairment. At 6 years old, a posterior spinal fusion was performed to treat severe kyphosis and scoliosis, and dental extractions were performed secondary to craniofacial structural abnormalities and associated dental complications. As the patient grew into adolescence, at 11 years old he was diagnosed with interstitial lung disease – a potential effect of the radiation he received before the prior bone marrow graft. At 13 years old, the patient underwent another posterior spinal fusion. As skeletal manifestations continued to progress from dysostosis multiplex, medial physeal stapling and ankle pinning were performed at 14 years old to combat genu valgum and secondary subtalar varus ( Fig. 1 A). 3.2 Chronology of adult clinical events As an adult, at age 19, the patient was diagnosed with aortic regurgitation and pectus excavatum ( Fig. 1 B). Progressive visual impairment continued, and the patient was diagnosed with corneal clouding at 21 years old. At 22 years old, the patient began exhibiting motor issues, slowed speech, and headaches, and physicians subsequently identified an atypical benign right sphenoid wing meningioma ( Fig. 2 A). The patient subsequently underwent two frontotemporal subtotal craniotomies nine days apart to remove most of the meningioma ( Fig. 2 B), while some residual tumor was knowingly left along the dural surface. At about this time, a systolic heart murmur was also detected. At 25 years old, genetic testing revealed PHE130LeuX3 and Trp402X IDUA mutations consistent with MPS IH, and growth of the residual sphenoid wing meningioma was noted. The following year, the patient was diagnosed with mildly thickened aortic and mitral valve leaflets, a paroxysmal neurological event, and chronic encephalomalacia. Dental intervention also continued, including an odontotomy for progressive dental pathology. At 27 years old, the patient was diagnosed with epilepsy after follow-up consultations regarding the paroxysmal event. At 28 years old, the patient was diagnosed with retinal dystrophy secondary to GAG deposits, and physicians identified a right post-temporal meningioma alongside additional intracranial lesions. Approximately six months later, the patient underwent gamma knife radiation targeting the right post-temporal meningioma, and radiographic imaging subsequently identified subchondral bone marrow edema. At age 30, the patient experienced right knee pain caused by an osteochondral lesion of the femur which was believed to be associated with persistent subchondral bone marrow edema. At 31 years old, the patient underwent an additional gamma knife radiation procedure for two meningiomas: one located in the right temporoparietal region and the other located inferolaterally in the middle cranial fossa. In many MRIs, the development and progression of a partially empty, J-shaped sella turcica and other anatomical signs of MPS IH were documented ( Fig. 3 ). At 32 years old, the patient began experiencing what was thought to be severe anxiety and panic attacks. Anti-anxiety medications were prescribed but were ineffective, so further medical discussion prompted search for other explanations. Subsequent MRI found an aggressive meningioma had developed and invaded the cranium, bone, and overlying skin, invoking seizure activity that was previously interpreted as anxiety and panic attacks. As this meningioma enveloped major vein, a craniotomy was warranted to resect the majority of the tumor. The patient experienced multiple post-surgical seizures, and the patient maintains an intellectual level approximately comparable to that of a 4-year-old ( Fig. 1 B). 4 Discussion 4.1 Progression of MPS IH disease burden into adulthood The patient's musculoskeletal implications, facial and dental variations, cardiopulmonary complications, visual impairments, and neurocognitive level are all within the scope of expected developments for MPS IH ( Fig. 1 ). However, it is evident that adult survivorship of MPS IH in the present case carries more numerous, irregular, and severe disease manifestations – particularly neuro-oncologic in nature and requiring recurrent surgical intervention – and other systematic manifestations that have not been formerly explicitly associated with MPS IH ( Fig. 1 B). While the patient's extended lifespan is credited to the early HSCT interventions, total body irradiation as conditioning required for those treatments is thought to predispose patients to meningioma development [64] , [87] , [88] , [89] . ERT may provoke immune responses against the recombinant enzyme that can reduce therapeutic efficacy. However, HSCT has been shown to mitigate these antibody responses by replacing the recipient's immune system with donor-derived immune cells [90] . Conversely, ERT is also effective as a bridging therapy to improve HSCT engraftment rates, supporting ERT's use as an adjunctive therapy to HSCT [91] . The increasing implementation of newborn screening programs for MPS I has enabled earlier diagnosis and referral for HSCT. Earlier diagnosis and treatment have been associated with improved long-term clinical outcomes and survival, suggesting that continued advances in screening and treatment may further improve longevity in patients with MPS IH [92] . Although little is known about the long-term outcomes of MPS IH, cases of iatrogenic meningioma and other iatrogenic complications have been reported secondary to childhood total body irradiation used as conditioning for HSCT [35] , [64] . While early transplant conditioning regimens utilized total body irradiation, such as in the current case, current regimens work to better achieve full donor chimerism with minimal side effects. Combination therapies using myeloablative drugs, such as busulfan and fludarabine or cyclophosphamide, may be used in conjunction with reduced-intensity conditioning in place of total body irradiation for HSCT conditioning. However, while myeloablative drugs such as busulfan achieve high chimerism, they are also associated with greater toxicity. Conversely, reduced-intensity conditioning decreases toxicity but is associated with a greater risk of graft failure. Researchers continue to work on new treatment options, such as antibody-based therapies, to leverage the benefits of HSCT for long-term survivorship of MPS with full donor chimerism and minimize side effects [35] . 4.2 Neurologic tumor burden and seizure risk Meningiomas and epilepsy represent a significant component of the adult neurologic disease burden in long-term MPS IH survivorship. These disorders reflect a convergence of metabolic vulnerability, tumor-driven structural disruptions, and cumulative surgical or radiation sequelae. After presenting with signs of a cranial lesion at 22 years old, the patient was diagnosed with the first of many benign meningiomas thought to be from the total body radiation treatment incurred over two decades prior. Radiation-induced meningiomas are known to be more aggressive, more resistant to intervention, and exhibit a higher rate of recurrence [87] , [88] . Meningiomas, while typically histologically benign, can exert profound neurologic effects due to mass effect and epileptogenic cortical disruption. Representing the most common intracranial tumor, 98% of meningiomas are non-malignant, yet up to 50% of affected individuals develop tumor-associated seizures, particularly when lesions involve the temporal lobe [89] , [93] . The patient underwent two right frontotemporal subtotal craniotomies with incomplete resection of a right sphenoid wing meningioma. Postoperative MRI demonstrated residual tumor irregularity along the right anterolateral temporal lobe ( Fig. 2 ) – the region most associated with focal seizure onset [94] , [95] . Subsequent neuroimaging revealed persistent tumor growth, chronic microhemorrhages, lacunar infarcts, increased intracranial pressure, and hydrocephalus. By 28 years old, a new post-temporal meningioma prompted gamma knife radiation – a treatment that was favored by the patient over craniotomy and excision. Additional gamma knife radiation was required at 31 years old to treat expanding temporoparietal and middle cranial fossa tumors, highlighting the chronic, recurrent tumor burden in adulthood. While emerging evidence implicates lysosomal storage diseases in disrupted autophagic flux, lysosomal dysfunction, and chronic inflammatory signaling that may promote pro-oncogenic cellular environments [96] , [97] , [98] , MPS I is not associated with meningioma development, and reported cases of such appear to be iatrogenic. Epilepsy is reported in approximately 30% of MPS patients overall, but cases predominantly involve MPS II and MPS III [99] , leaving a critical gap in knowledge regarding the seizure burden of MPS IH survivors. However, structural aberrations and post-surgical changes present in many MPS IH patients confer high epileptogenic risk [95] , [100] . Additionally, GAG accumulation in the brain is hypothesized to alter neuronal signaling, suggesting a metabolic contribution common to MPS IH patients [99] . Following a solitary focal impaired-awareness seizure at 26 years old, the patient was diagnosed with focal epilepsy which was subsequently managed with antiepileptic therapy. This patient's seizure risk profile is multifactorial, influenced by a history of recurring meningiomas and temporal lobe lesions. Although the patient experienced only a single reported focal seizure approximately four years after the first two craniotomies, the patient remained seizure-free with continued antiepileptic pharmacological management until the later development and resection of the higher grade (more invasive) meningioma. 4.3 Chronic cardiopulmonary morbidity Cardiopulmonary disease represents a persistent source of morbidity in MPS IH, particularly in individuals who survive into adulthood with preserved functional capacity. Systemic cardiovascular complications are prevalent among MPS IH cases [44] , [46] , [48] . The aortic regurgitation with mild mitral and aortic valve thickening that the patient was diagnosed with in early adulthood are both well-characterized cardiovascular manifestations associated with MPS I [13] , [48] . The patient's medical records also noted a localized apical pericardial effusion and spontaneous septal defect closure, and the patient's right ventricle showed mild compression secondary to pectus excavatum – a common thoracic deformity in MPS IH [44] . Although diffuse coronary narrowing is recognized as a severe and potentially fatal cardiovascular complication in untreated MPS IH, the patient has maintained preserved systolic function and remains under longitudinal cardiology surveillance [46] , [48] . Although the patient's carotid intima-media thickness measurement was not available, this conclusion aligns with current research. HSCT treatments may provide significant benefits to GAG-related vasculopathy; however, they do not fully halt disease progression [47] . Despite structural cardiac aberrations, the patient maintains an active daily routine lifestyle without evidence of functional limitation. Restrictive pulmonary disease remains a major contributor to respiratory morbidity. The patient's medical records confirmed severe restrictive lung disease, a clinically significant complication commonly driven by ribcage dysplasia, diaphragmatic restriction from hepatosplenomegaly, and airway cartilage thickening from MPS IH [101] , [102] . Interstitial lung disease is also common among MPS IH patients, and the impact of the disease secondary to HSCT treatment should be underscored. Following the second attempt at HSCT, the patient notably required persistent oxygen supplementation via nasal canula until he was 3 years old. No ongoing supplemental oxygen requirement has been necessary outside of the postoperative recovery timeframe, and pulmonary status has remained stable without limiting dyspnea. The patient has since tolerated multiple procedures without pulmonary complications, demonstrating preserved day-to-day functional capacity despite a significant cumulative cardiopulmonary disease burden. The patient has a documented history of difficult intubation, consistent with an anatomically restricted airway associated with GAG-associated tracheal remodeling, which poses a well-established anesthetic risk in patients with MPS IH [13] , [44] , [102] , [103] . Subsequent intubations were performed successfully though, highlighting procedural feasibility despite the persistent risk. Sjøgren et al. [44] describe pre- and post-operative considerations for MPS patients needing anesthesia. In their article, the authors describe the need for thorough clinical evaluation as MPS-associated anatomical variations can complicate intubation, cause bleeding, and elicit stagnation of secretions. The authors recommend treating MPS patients with lung physiotherapy, positive end-expiratory pressure, and antibiotics to prevent postoperative complications caused by pre-existing MPS conditions. Chronic middle ear effusions, repeatedly documented in the patient's medical record, also reflect upper airway involvement in eustachian tube dysfunction [102] . 4.4 Musculoskeletal disease burden Dysostosis multiplex represents a lifelong, progressive MPS IH skeletal disease burden from the failure of primary ossification which continues into adulthood despite early intervention [32] . Significant manifestations in this patient include genu valgum, hip dysplasia, scoliosis, carpal tunnel syndrome, and dental abnormalities, reflecting a persistent skeletal burden characteristic of adult survivorship in MPS IH. Regardless of HSCT, genu valgum develops in about 52% of MPS IH patients in the first 2–5 years of life [104] due to failure of primary ossification at the proximal tibial metaphysis [32] . Epiphyseal stapling of the knees and ankle pinning are standard practices for preventing secondary complications, including lateral compartment arthritis and secondary subtalar varus [104] . By age 29, the patient required physical therapy for continued mobility, as an osteochondral lesion of the femur associated with subchondral bone marrow edema contributed to joint pain during ambulation. This development is also indicative of early-onset osteoarthritis. Medical records indicate right hip dysplasia has been present since childhood without corrective surgical intervention, representing a source of ongoing hip instability. Acetabular dysplasia is a common manifestation in MPS IH patients and rarely improves in the absence of surgical intervention [103] . In patients treated with HSCT who exceed 10-years, GAG deposition within articular surfaces, such as the acetabulum, contributes to progressive adult joint degeneration [105] . Spinal disease further illustrates the incomplete protection conferred by HSCT and early interventions. The patient underwent two posterior spinal fusions at the ages of 6 and 13 years old for kyphosis and scoliosis, and they still required subsequent physical therapy. Despite HSCT, a high prevalence of scoliosis (81%) and kyphosis (32.6%) is evident in MPS IH patient populations [32] , [106] . These skeletal deformities compound adult cardiopulmonary strain and negatively impact respiratory functions, underscoring some of the multi-system functional consequences of skeletal disease [35] . Peripheral neuropathy is another longitudinal burden of musculoskeletal disorders. GAG accumulation in the flexor retinaculum causes inflammation which leads to median nerve compression and carpal tunnel syndrome, as seen in the present case and in 63.3% of MPS IH patients [32] . Although incidence is negatively correlated with early HSCT and ERT, diagnostic delays usually persist due to communication barriers [107] . 4.5 Other considerations The patient's medical records noted corneal opacities and clouding, bilateral corneal deposits, and a tortuous left optic nerve with a mildly dilated nerve sheath. When the patient was 5 years old, he underwent cataract surgery, resulting in bilateral pseudophakia. These represent common ocular complications of MPS IH [55] , [56] and may contribute to the ongoing visual impairment in the patient. Additionally, MRI revealed a J-shaped sella turcica and a partially empty sella ( Fig. 3 ). Empty sella describes an intrasellar herniation of the subarachnoid space with pituitary gland flattening [108] , [109] . Documentation of empty sella findings in MPS IH patients is limited, and this case may represent an incidental finding. However, the patient has reported neurological consequences consistent with empty sella syndrome, including headache, dizziness, and optic nerve compression. These symptoms may indicate a case of empty sella syndrome secondary to surgery, or incidental findings from comorbid conditions such as hydrocephalus or increased intracranial pressure. Regardless, the partial empty sella finding may prompt the patient's healthcare team to watch for signs of pituitary-associated endocrinologic disruption among the more predictable sequelae associated with MPS IH [110] . 4.6 Comparative cases A very limited number of publications describe individuals with MPS IH surviving into adulthood, and of those that do, most focus on specific orthopedic or surgical outcomes rather than the holistic, multisystem burden of the disease. Kennedy et al. [105] evaluated hip outcomes in adult patients, including a 23-year-old with acetabular dysplasia and degenerative hip changes. As aforementioned, Kennedy et al. [105] noted that even after surgical correction, most patients demonstrated significant functional limitations and an increased risk of early arthritis. Wyffels et al. [111] describe a 23-year-old who received HSCT treatment and later endured peripheral nerve morbidity via carpal tunnel syndrome which required repeated surgical intervention and resulted in residual stiffness and motor limitations persisting into adulthood. Beyond orthopedic and neurological sequelae, Regalbuto and Klenotic [112] present a case of a 32-year-old patient with MPS IH who developed metastatic breast cancer following childhood total body irradiation for HSCT conditioning. As somewhat similar to meningioma development in the current patient case analysis, this study notably reports another example of oncologic risk secondary to early childhood total body irradiation rather than from the MPS disease. While such treatment may be indicated for HSCT conditioning, other techniques may be explored to minimize later-life complications as adult life expectancy increases in MPS IH patients. Collectively, these few reports reveal a pattern of persistent, progressive complications associated with long-term survival in MPS IH patients. The scarcity and narrow scope of existing cases highlight a substantial gap in understanding the longitudinal phenotype of MPS IH survivors and emphasize the need for greater attention to adult disease burden beyond orthopedic manifestations. 4.7 Study limitations The main limitation of the present study is the limited information available about adult-stage MPS IH due to the disease's late diagnosis, early treatment necessity, severity, and short lifespan of afflicted patients. While the present case provides information about a single adult patient with MPS IH, the limited availability of other adult MPS IH case reports restricts meaningful comparisons between similar patients' treatments and disease burden histories, reducing the current ability to broadly contextualize findings within established adult-stage MPS IH disease patterns. Additionally, retrospective case review is subject to limitations in data uniformity as record interpretations are subject to availability of records, thoroughness of documentation by a widespread healthcare team, and corroboration by the patient's primary caregivers. To situate the case within the scope of existing knowledge about MPS IH, the authors conducted a focused literature review to contextualize the case within the broader clinical perspective. The resulting introduction provided foundational information about MPS IH which identified a significant gap in knowledge, justifying the purpose and necessary effort for conducting the review. Incorporating a relevant, rare-case analysis validates the purpose of the study and counterbalances the study's limitations with important evidential translational insights about the expected disease burden for MPS IH patients with expectedly extended lifespans. 5 Conclusions While historically considered a pediatric disease, modern advances in MPS IH treatment options have been shown to extend patient lifespans into adulthood; however, MPS IH survivorship and long-term MPS IH progression consequently remain minimally described, especially regarding new sequelae developed by adult MPS IH patients. This study provides a foundational, literature-based review of MPS I disorders aimed at providing specific insight about the adult disease burden of MPS IH. An especially relevant case of a 32-year-old survivor of MPS IH is presented to contextualize the importance of addressing the gap in knowledge about early treatment intervention and the adult-stage disease burden of MPS IH. The medical record review and chronological mapping of comorbidities provided context for important discussion about persistent knowledge gaps and the adult disease burden of MPS IH survivors. The findings of this study illustrate that while early treatments may extend life expectancy, they do not prevent progressive development of common sequelae or adult stage developments, particularly neuro-oncologic in nature. While this study provides important insights about early interventional treatment and long-term surveillance strategies for MPS IH survivors, it also underscores the need for expanded reporting adult MPS IH disease presentation and clinical sequelae to further improve treatment and quality of life for MPS IH patients and their families. This study may enhance physician awareness about the multisystem disease burden of adult-stage patients with MPS IH, improve treatment and care options for patients with MPS IH, and support clinical counseling for families facing long-term clinical management of MPS IH.
